description: We are currently welcoming passionate teammates with skills in Coding, Software & Web Development, Game Design, Graphic Design, Storytelling, and Mars-related exploration. If you are excited about building out-of-this-world experiences, join us!
summary:
TARUKH is a browser-based 3D Mars exploration and mission-training game designed for children aged 7–12. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge’s “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer,” it turns space science into practical activities where young explorers observe, experiment, solve problems and make decisions.

We developed a playable Martian environment containing an accessible outpost, six cultivation greenhouses, solar equipment, a rover garage and a driveable crew rover with working cockpit displays. Players can explore freely or follow the seven-mission Elysium Outpost story, preparing a habitat for its next crew. Activities include repairing electrical connections, cleaning solar panels, connecting water systems, calibrating sensors, comparing plant-growing conditions, planning rover journeys

TARUKH addresses the challenge by connecting each activity to a junior astronaut skill: observation, troubleshooting, resource planning, navigation, preparedness and reflection. Short instructions, visual feedback, optional science explanations and a mission journal help children understand why their choices matter. Guided missions support pause, saved progress and retries, allowing players to learn at their own pace.
details:
TARUKH is an interactive, browser-based Mars exploration and mission-training game designed for children aged 7–12. Our goal is to help young explorers understand what astronauts must observe, maintain and plan to live and work beyond Earth. The project combines a navigable 3D environment, practical science activities and a guided story grounded in NASA resources.

Players can choose Free Exploration or the seven-mission Elysium Outpost story. In the story, they help astronaut Kaelen Reeves prepare a Mars base for its next crew. They explore the habitat, greenhouses, solar equipment and garage, interact with nearby stations, and complete activities that affect their operating plan. Clear next-step instructions, optional science explanations and a mission journal connect individual tasks to the expedition’s wider objectives.

The activities cover several aspects of junior astronaut preparation:

- Energy: repair electrical connections, brush dust from solar panels and allocate power between essential systems.

- Life support: connect water-treatment systems, calibrate instruments and manage water recovery, oxygen generation and carbon dioxide removal as separate processes.

- Food production: compare plant trials and consider how light, water and electricity affect cultivation.

- Exploration: plan a rover journey, check battery reserves, restore a field sensor, collect samples and examine their visible characteristics.

- Preparedness: review a historical solar event, inspect shelter ventilation and power, and compare simulated shielding options.

- Integrated planning: submit an operating plan, respond to an equipment fault and revise decisions during a retryable overnight readiness exercise.

The environment makes these activities tangible. Players can walk through the outpost, enter cultivation greenhouses and drive a crew rover with a furnished cockpit. Its displays show simulated speed, battery and charging information, navigation and wheel diagnostics. A minimap and regional atlas support orientation, while contextual interactions connect the world’s equipment to the learning activities.

Scientific data is part of the experience. The terrain uses NASA Mars Global Surveyor’s Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter elevation data, with a region selected through Mars Trek. Distances are compressed and relief is exaggerated to make exploration practical. NASA research on life-support systems, plant cultivation and solar-panel dust informs the activities. The radiation phone fetches live NOAA near-Earth proton observations and provides simulated historical-event replays using NASA DONKI references. We distinguish these observations and historical records from the game’s authored Mars exposure and resource models.

The intended benefits include scientific curiosity, spatial awareness, problem-solving, data literacy and systems thinking. A child can discover that producing oxygen requires water and electricity, that growing crops competes for resources, and that a rover expedition needs enough energy for the return journey. The mission journal encourages players to explain their choices and reflect on what they learned. These are intended educational outcomes; classroom and child playtesting would be needed to measure learning gains.

Our development tools and technologies include:

- TypeScript and JavaScript for simulation, interactions and application logic.

- React for menus, mission interfaces, instruments and learning activities.

- Three.js and WebGL for 3D rendering, lighting, animation and cameras.

- HTML, CSS and Tailwind CSS for interface styling and responsive layouts.

- Blender and asset-processing scripts for model assembly and preparation, with GLB assets, Draco geometry compression and WebP textures.

- Vite, Git and GitHub for builds, version control and collaboration, with Vercel hosting the submitted game.

- Codex & Antigravity-assisted development, automated tests, TypeScript checks, production builds and browser checks for implementation and validation.

The project’s creativity comes from connecting scientific concepts within one explorable world. A solar-panel activity contributes to an energy plan; that plan influences life support, cultivation and rover preparation. The radiation phone brings space-weather information into a familiar interface, while the rover cockpit turns navigation and resource monitoring into part of the experience.

Our team considered age-appropriate instructions, keyboard and touch access, reduced-motion support, readable feedback, saved progress and opportunities to retry. We also considered device limitations through adjustable graphics, compressed assets, shared geometry and bounded terrain rendering. Scientific accuracy, transparent simulation assumptions and asset attribution were central considerations. TARUKH aims to make astronaut-style observation and decision-making approachable through an engaging learning experience.
